rows.stem: The number of solutions of differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y = 1\), given that y(0) = 1, is :
rows.solution: Solve it and count. The equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} - y = 1\) is linear with \(P = -1\), so \(\text{I.F.} = e^{-x}\) and \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(y e^{-x}\right) = e^{-x}\). Integrating, \(y e^{-x} = -e^{-x} + c\), so the general solution is \(y = c e^{x} - 1\), a family with ONE arbitrary constant. The initial condition \(y(0) = 1\) forces \(1 = c - 1\), so \(c = 2\) and \(y = 2e^{x} - 1\) — a single curve. Hence exactly \(1\) solution, which is the choice \(1\). (This is the general principle: a first-order equation has a one-parameter family of solutions, and one initial condition pins the parameter down to a unique member.)

rows.stem: The number of all scalar matrices of order 3, with each entry \(-1\), 0 or 1, is :
rows.solution: A scalar matrix is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are all EQUAL, so a scalar matrix of order 3 has the form \(kI = \begin{bmatrix} k & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & k & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & k \end{bmatrix}\). It is therefore determined by the single number \(k\), and the off-diagonal entries are forced to be \(0\) — which is one of the permitted values, so every such choice is admissible. Since \(k\) may be \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\), there are exactly \(3\) such matrices, matching the choice \(3\). (The value \(3^9\) counts ALL \(3 \times 3\) matrices with entries from that set, ignoring the scalar condition entirely.)

Apply the chain rule with the inner function \(u = \log x + e^{x}\). Then \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos u = -\sin u \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\), where \(\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{1}{x} + e^{x}\). So the derivative is \(-\sin(\log x + e^{x})\left(\frac{1}{x} + e^{x}\right)\). Now put \(x = 1\): the inner function is \(\log 1 + e^{1} = 0 + e = e\), and the bracket is \(\frac{1}{1} + e^{1} = 1 + e\). Hence the value is \(-(1 + e)\sin e\), matching the choice \(-(1 + e)\sin e\). (Forgetting the chain-rule factor gives \(-\sin e\), which is why that also appears among the choices.)

rows.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about equivalence classes \(A_i\) (i = 1, 2, .... n) formed by an equivalence relation R defined on a set A ?

options.label: D
options.text: All elements of \(A_i\) are related to each other, for all i

rows.solution:
The equivalence classes of a relation PARTITION the set: they cover it and they are pairwise DISJOINT. Checking the four statements against that: the union of all the classes is indeed the whole of \(A\), so that one is true; if \(x\) lies in both \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) then those classes coincide, so that one is true; and every two members of one class are related, since a class is exactly the set of elements related to a given one, so that one is true as well. The remaining statement, \(A_i \cap A_j 
e \phi\) for \(i 
e j\), asserts that two DIFFERENT classes overlap, which contradicts disjointness — for distinct classes \(A_i \cap A_j = \phi\). Since the question asks which statement is NOT true, the answer is the choice \(A_i \cap A_j 
e \phi, i 
e j\).

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.stem: If \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 2 e^{2x}\, dx = \int_0^a e^x\, dx\), the value of 'a' is :
rows.solution: Evaluate the two sides and equate. Left side: \(\int_0^2 2e^{2x}\,dx = \left[e^{2x}\right]_0^2 = e^4 - 1\), since \(\frac{d}{dx}e^{2x} = 2e^{2x}\) so the factor \(2\) is exactly what the antiderivative needs. Right side: \(\int_0^a e^{x}\,dx = \left[e^{x}\right]_0^a = e^{a} - 1\). Equating, \(e^{a} - 1 = e^{4} - 1\), so \(e^{a} = e^{4}\) and, the exponential being one-one, \(a = 4\). This is the choice \(4\).

Notice that \(x^6 = (x^3)^2\) and that \(x^2\,dx\) is, up to a constant, the differential of \(x^3\). So put \(x^3 = t\), giving \(3x^2\,dx = dt\), that is \(x^2\,dx = \frac{dt}{3}\). The limits become \(t = 0\) when \(x = 0\) and \(t = (a^3)^3 = a^9\) when \(x = a^3\). The integral turns into \(\frac{1}{3}\int_0^{a^9} \frac{dt}{t^2 + (a^3)^2}\). Using \(\int \frac{dt}{t^2 + p^2} = \frac{1}{p}\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{p}\) with \(p = a^3\), this is \(\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{a^3}\left[\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{a^3}\right]_0^{a^9} = \frac{1}{3a^3}\left(\tan^{-1} a^6 - \tan^{-1} 0\right)\). Since \(\tan^{-1} 0 = 0\), the value is \(\frac{1}{3a^3}\tan^{-1}\left(a^6\right)\).

rows.stem: Check the differentiability of \(f(x) = |\cos x|\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
rows.solution: The modulus changes formula exactly where \(\cos x\) changes sign, and \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) is such a point, so remove the modulus on either side of it: \(f(x) = \cos x\) for \(0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2}\) (where \(\cos x \ge 0\)) and \(f(x) = -\cos x\) for \(\frac{\pi}{2} \le x \le \pi\) (where \(\cos x \le 0\)). Note \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0\). Left-hand derivative: \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - h\right) - f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{-h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - h\right) - 0}{-h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{-h} = -1\), using \(\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{\sin h}{h} = 1\). Right-hand derivative: \(\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + h\right) - f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + h\right) - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1\). Since the left-hand derivative \(-1\) is not equal to the right-hand derivative \(1\), the function \(f(x) = |\cos x|\) is NOT differentiable at \(x = \frac{\pi}{2}\). (It IS continuous there — the graph has a corner, not a jump.)

rows.stem: If \(y = A \sin 2x + B \cos 2x\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} - ky = 0\), find the value of k.
rows.solution: Differentiate twice and compare with the given equation. First, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2A\cos 2x - 2B\sin 2x\). Differentiating again, \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -4A\sin 2x - 4B\cos 2x = -4\left(A\sin 2x + B\cos 2x\right) = -4y\). So the function satisfies \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 4y = 0\). Comparing this with the given \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - ky = 0\), we need \(-k = 4\), so \(k = -4\). (The relation holds for every choice of the constants \(A\) and \(B\), which is why \(k\) is a single definite number and not an expression in them.)

rows.stem: If vectors \(\vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\) and \(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}\) are unit vectors, then find the angle between \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\).
rows.solution: Being unit vectors, \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = |2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}| = 1\). Square the third condition, using \(|\vec{u}|^2 = \vec{u} \cdot \vec{u}\): \(|2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}|^2 = 4|\vec{a}|^2 + 12\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + 9|\vec{b}|^2 = 1\). Substituting \(|\vec{a}|^2 = |\vec{b}|^2 = 1\) gives \(4 + 12\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + 9 = 1\), so \(12\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -12\) and \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = -1\). Now \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\cos\theta = \cos\theta\), so \(\cos\theta = -1\) and hence \(\theta = \pi\), that is \(180^{\circ}\). The two vectors are therefore antiparallel. (This is consistent: \(\cos\theta = -1\) forces \(\vec{b} = -\vec{a}\), and then \(2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} = -\vec{a}\), whose magnitude is indeed \(1\).)

The relation is a product of high powers, so take logarithms first to turn products into sums. Taking \(\log\) of both sides, \(30\log x + 20\log y = 50\log(x + y)\). Differentiating with respect to \(x\), remembering the chain rule on \(y\) and on \(x + y\): \(\frac{30}{x} + \frac{20}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{50}{x + y}\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right)\). Collect the derivative terms on the left and the rest on the right: \(\frac{dy}{dx}\left(\frac{20}{y} - \frac{50}{x + y}\right) = \frac{50}{x + y} - \frac{30}{x}\). Combining each side over a common denominator, the left bracket is \(\frac{20(x + y) - 50y}{y(x + y)} = \frac{20x - 30y}{y(x + y)}\) and the right side is \(\frac{50x - 30(x + y)}{x(x + y)} = \frac{20x - 30y}{x(x + y)}\). So \(\frac{dy}{dx} \cdot \frac{20x - 30y}{y(x + y)} = \frac{20x - 30y}{x(x + y)}\). Cancelling the common factor \(\frac{20x - 30y}{x + y}\) leaves \(\frac{dy}{dx} \cdot \frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{x}\), that is \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x}\), as required.

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
rows.solution: Differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), using \(\frac{d}{dx}5^{u} = 5^{u}\log 5 \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\): \(5^{x}\log 5 + 5^{y}\log 5 \, \frac{dy}{dx} = 5^{x+y}\log 5\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right)\). Cancel the common factor \(\log 5\), and then use the GIVEN relation to replace \(5^{x+y}\) by \(5^{x} + 5^{y}\): \(5^{x} + 5^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(5^{x} + 5^{y}\right)\left(1 + \frac{dy}{dx}\right)\). Expanding the right side, \(5^{x} + 5^{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = 5^{x} + 5^{x}\frac{dy}{dx} + 5^{y} + 5^{y}\frac{dy}{dx}\). The terms \(5^{x}\) and \(5^{y}\frac{dy}{dx}\) cancel from both sides, leaving \(0 = 5^{x}\frac{dy}{dx} + 5^{y}\). Hence \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{5^{y}}{5^{x}} = -5^{\,y-x}\).

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem:
Find the value of p for which the lines

\(\vec{r} = \lambda\hat{i} + (2\lambda + 1)\hat{j} + (3\lambda + 2)\hat{k}\) and

\(\vec{r} = \hat{i} - 3\mu\hat{j} + (p\mu + 7)\hat{k}\)

are perpendicular to each other and also intersect. Also, find the point of intersection of the given lines.
rows.solution: Read each line as a point plus a direction. The first is \(\vec{r} = \hat{j} + 2\hat{k} + \lambda(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k})\), with direction \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\); the second is \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + 7\hat{k} + \mu(-3\hat{j} + p\hat{k})\), with direction \(-3\hat{j} + p\hat{k}\). Perpendicularity means the dot product of the directions vanishes: \((\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) \cdot (-3\hat{j} + p\hat{k}) = 0 + 2(-3) + 3p = -6 + 3p = 0\), so \(p = 2\). Now check that they really meet, and find where. A general point of the first line is \((\lambda,\; 2\lambda + 1,\; 3\lambda + 2)\) and of the second (with \(p = 2\)) is \((1,\; -3\mu,\; 2\mu + 7)\). Equating coordinates gives \(\lambda = 1\), \(2\lambda + 1 = -3\mu\) and \(3\lambda + 2 = 2\mu + 7\). The first two give \(\lambda = 1\) and \(3 = -3\mu\), so \(\mu = -1\); substituting into the third gives \(5 = 5\), which holds, so the lines do intersect. Putting \(\lambda = 1\) into the first line, the point of intersection is \((1, 3, 5)\). Hence \(p = 2\) and the lines meet at \((1, 3, 5)\).

rows.subtopic: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
rows.solution: Use the reversal law \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\); since \(B^{-1}\) is already given, only \(A^{-1}\) has to be computed. Expanding along the first row, \(|A| = 5(3 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2) - 0 + 4(2 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 1) = 5(-1) + 4(1) = -1 \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists. The cofactors are \(A_{11} = -1\), \(A_{12} = 0\), \(A_{13} = 1\), \(A_{21} = 8\), \(A_{22} = 1\), \(A_{23} = -10\), \(A_{31} = -12\), \(A_{32} = -2\), \(A_{33} = 15\). Transposing the cofactor matrix, \(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 8 & -12 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -10 & 15 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \frac{\text{adj}\,A}{|A|} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -8 & 12 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 10 & -15 \end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying, \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -8 & 12 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 10 & -15 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 19 & -27 \\ -2 & 18 & -25 \\ -3 & 29 & -42 \end{bmatrix}\). For the determinant there is no need to expand this product: \(\left|(AB)^{-1}\right| = \left|B^{-1}\right|\left|A^{-1}\right|\), and \(\left|B^{-1}\right| = 1(16 - 9) - 3(4 - 3) + 3(3 - 4) = 7 - 3 - 3 = 1\) while \(\left|A^{-1}\right| = \frac{1}{|A|} = -1\). Hence \(\left|(AB)^{-1}\right| = 1 \times (-1) = -1\).

rows.stem:
Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), find \(A^{-1}\). Use it to solve the following system of equations :

\(x + y + z = 1\)

\(2x + 3y + 2z = 2\)

\(x + y + 2z = 4\)
rows.solution: Expanding along the first row, \(|A| = 1(3 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 1) - 1(2 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 1) + 1(2 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 1) = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1 \ne 0\), so \(A^{-1}\) exists and the system has a unique solution. The cofactors are \(A_{11} = 4\), \(A_{12} = -2\), \(A_{13} = -1\), \(A_{21} = -1\), \(A_{22} = 1\), \(A_{23} = 0\), \(A_{31} = -1\), \(A_{32} = 0\), \(A_{33} = 1\). Transposing gives \(\text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), and since \(|A| = 1\), \(A^{-1} = \text{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The system is exactly \(AX = B\) with \(X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\), because the coefficient matrix of the three equations is the given \(A\). Hence \(X = A^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 - 2 - 4 \\ -2 + 2 + 0 \\ -1 + 0 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\). So \(x = -2\), \(y = 0\), \(z = 3\). Checking in the original equations: \(-2 + 0 + 3 = 1\), \(-4 + 0 + 6 = 2\), and \(-2 + 0 + 6 = 4\), all as required.
